publicationLaw: Only source-grounded objects that point into the existing shared ATLAS may be indexable. These pages explain the data and its limits; they do not create a second map or truth system.

objects.title: Earth — Explore the living planet in 4PLANET ATLAS
objects.name: Earth
objects.description: Explore Earth through source-grounded satellite imagery and planetary layers in 4PLANET ATLAS, with source dates, limitations and direct access to the live map.
objects.summary: Start with the whole planet. 4PLANET ATLAS brings public planetary data into one shared interface so a person can move from Earth-scale context towards places, species, events and human systems.
objects.whyItMatters: Planetary data is often fragmented across specialist services. This object gives a human-readable entry point into the existing ATLAS without hiding where the underlying data comes from.
availableData: NASA Blue Marble as the stable global base view
Daily or near-daily NASA imagery and scientific layers where the source supports it
Biodiversity, ocean, land, climate, event and human-system layers inside the same ATLAS
objects.freshness: Each ATLAS layer has its own time semantics. Blue Marble is a composite base; dated scientific layers must be read with their displayed source date.
limitations: The map is an interface over multiple sources with different coverage and update cadences.
A visible layer is not automatically live or complete.
Absence of a record or signal is not evidence of ecological absence.

sources.label: NASA Global Imagery Browse Services (GIBS)
sources.use: Source documentation for the Blue Marble and NASA imagery layers used by ATLAS.

objects.title: Global Fires — Satellite thermal anomalies in 4PLANET ATLAS
objects.name: Global Fires
objects.description: Explore recent global satellite thermal anomalies and source-reported open events in 4PLANET ATLAS. A heat detection is not automatically a confirmed wildfire.
objects.summary: See where recent heat signals are being detected across the planet, then inspect them in the shared ATLAS alongside other planetary layers.
objects.whyItMatters: Fire information spreads quickly and is easy to overstate. 4PLANET keeps the signal and the interpretation separate: satellite thermal anomalies show detected heat, while source-reported event feeds describe events under their own definitions.
availableData: NASA GIBS MODIS Terra thermal-anomaly imagery used by the existing global ATLAS fire layer
NASA EONET source-reported open natural-event records in the existing ATLAS event layer
Direct comparison with other ATLAS context such as vegetation, forest loss and Earth imagery
objects.freshness: The current ATLAS fire raster requests a recent configured NASA GIBS date. EONET records retain the source feed's event status. Read the source date and event definition before treating either as current local conditions.
limitations: A thermal anomaly is detected heat, not proof of a wildfire.
An EONET event marked open is not automatically an active local emergency.
Cloud, satellite coverage, source latency and source definitions can affect what appears.

objects.title: Whales — Explore reported cetacean observations in 4PLANET ATLAS
objects.name: Whales
objects.description: Explore a bounded set of reported whale and dolphin occurrence records in 4PLANET ATLAS, then move into source-grounded species profiles such as Orca.
objects.summary: Whales leave records across many datasets, not a single live track. The current ATLAS whale layer exposes a bounded OBIS occurrence slice so users can explore reported cetacean records while keeping the source limitations visible.
objects.whyItMatters: Dots on a map are seductive. They can also be misleading. This object makes the distinction explicit: occurrence records show reported observations or samples, not live positions, migration routes, population size or abundance.
availableData: Current public ATLAS whale layer backed by an OBIS Cetacea occurrence query
Map exploration of reported cetacean records with the existing shared ATLAS
Direct route into the curated Orca SPECIES object for deeper source-grounded context
objects.freshness: The current public ATLAS whale layer is a bounded broad Cetacea query and does not represent the complete OBIS record universe. Individual records carry their own observation dates and source context.
limitations: Occurrence records are not live animal positions.
Occurrence points do not form a migration route.
Record count is not abundance or population size.
The current broad ATLAS query is bounded and therefore incomplete.

sources.label: Ocean Biodiversity Information System API
sources.use: Primary source family for the current public ATLAS Cetacea occurrence layer.
